title: The Man Who Can’t Take a Break From Himself
author: William Meller
summary: Meller reflects on why a driven person who is tired still feels guilty about resting. Prompted by Sertillanges's The Intellectual Life, he first reads it as a call for better schedules, then realises it also speaks of sacrifice and rest. He distinguishes two kinds of discipline: resisting the urge to do nothing, and resisting the urge to keep going even when the work is good. The deeper problem, he suggests, is that activities such as writing and reading harden into identity cards, so that stopping feels like becoming less of who you believe you are. He observes that we even justify rest by its usefulness for tomorrow's performance. His modest alternative is to leave a book closed, not turn the next idea into a project, and accept that an afternoon may produce nothing worth counting.
points: Self-driven ambition can become its own taskmaster, so the leader has to practise the discipline of stopping as well as starting.
When an activity becomes identity, rest registers as a threat to the self rather than as maintenance.
Justifying rest purely by the performance it enables keeps even leisure on trial and leaves no space for real rest.
Wanting to do more is not the problem; losing the freedom to stop is.
Choosing one worthwhile thing means accepting that others are left undone, which no time management technique can remove.
quotes: Waking up tired should be a good enough reason to slow down. But then I think about the books I want to read, the subjects I still want to study, the ideas waiting to become articles, and suddenly resting starts to feel like a rather irresponsible decision.

Because, in my mind, discipline has almost always meant resisting the desire to do nothing. But there is another kind of discipline that may be just as important: resisting the desire to continue, even when what we’re doing is good.
People who write enjoy writing. People who read enjoy reading. Nothing strange so far. But at some point, an activity can become something like an identity card.

Sleep so we can perform better tomorrow. Go for a walk to organize our thoughts. Take a vacation to come back with more energy. All reasonable, of course, but why does even a quiet afternoon need to prove its value?
Maybe that’s part of the problem. If everything we do must contribute to the person we want to become, even stopping starts to look suspicious.

Not turning the next interesting idea into another project. Resting without having to come back better, smarter, or more prepared. And accepting, for a few hours, that I might not produce anything worth counting.
After all, there’s one rather inconvenient question left: if you stop doing all these things for a day, are you still the person you believe you are?
